rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3: two-year split-plot field experiment (2018-2020) at Ludhiana with three N levels and seven drip regimes, own measurements of soil moisture, ET, LAI, root mass density, N uptake and tuber yield.
rows.notes: The study does not measure nitrate leaching or ammonia volatilization under drip fertigation. Deep drainage in the water balance was assumed zero when storage was below field capacity (Section 2.2) and Tables 5-6 report drainage = 0 for all treatments; tensiometer data at 60-90 cm are said to indicate no drainage (Section 3.1). It reports N uptake by biomass and tubers (Tables 12-13), and only speculates that rain after a fertigation 'might have leached' N in 2019-2020. All treatments used 16 weekly fertigation splits, so no comparison of split vs non-split or drip vs non-drip on N loss exists. At most the absence of drainage flux under drip is a precondition for low leaching, hence upstream.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3, two-year field experiment with own measurements. Q2: Section 3.3 and Figure 2: subsurface drip treatments had their highest root mass density in the 15-30 cm layer (40-43% of total RMD) whereas surface drip (I7) concentrated 65% of roots in 0-15 cm; Section 3.4 and Table 10: tuber yield in I1-I3 was at par with or higher than I7, and Section 3.5 / Tables 12-13: tuber N uptake in I1-I3 significantly higher than I7; authors attribute the higher yield to greater RMD at 15-30 cm leading to more N uptake. Q4: intermediate variables measured - soil moisture by depth (Tables 3-4), soil matric potential (Figure 1), root mass density by depth (Figure 2), N uptake (Tables 12-13), transpiration (Table 7), with regressions of yield on transpiration (Figure 6, R2 = 0.92). Q9: Tables 8-13 report standard errors for LAI, DMA, tuber yield, tuber weight and N uptake; Table 10 gives SE and LSD for tuber yield.
rows.notes: Evidence is a comparison of subsurface drip (dripline at 20 cm) against surface drip; there is no non-drip (furrow) control, so the study shows that placing drip water deeper shifts roots deeper and raises N uptake and yield relative to surface drip, not that drip per se improves roots relative to conventional irrigation. Single site, single sandy loam soil, one cultivar; no triangulation (root cores only); no limitations stated; irrigation amount affects RMD and yield (I5, I6 lowest) but this is reported as a gradient, not stated as a requirement; RMD figure has letter groupings only, but yield/N-uptake SEs are given.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3: own two-year field experiment on potato under subsurface and surface drip.
rows.notes: The study measures no weed growth, disease incidence or foliage wetness. It does report (Section 3.1, Tables 3-4) that the 0-10 cm surface layer stayed relatively dry under subsurface drip and wet under surface drip, which is at most a precondition for the weed-germination mechanism in the passage; weed and disease outcomes are not assessed. Also the passage's cited sentence about planning/maintenance of drip in sandy soils is not studied either.

notes: Full text available, some OCR duplication in Sections 3.1 and 3.4 but content readable. Study is a plot-scale two-year field trial on one sandy loam site in Punjab comparing subsurface vs surface drip under three N levels; it measures water balance (drainage assumed zero), ET partitioning, LAI, DMA, root mass density, N uptake, tuber yield and water productivity, with no nitrate leaching, weed or disease measurements.
